expansion:
A. Orbital floor is correct. This is the classic presentation of an orbital-floor blow-out fracture after blunt orbital trauma. The lecture specifically labels this injury “Blunt trauma: Blow-out fracture of the orbital floor” and lists trauma from a “FIST, TENNIS BALL” as the history (L25, slide 19; L25, slide 20). It explains that diplopia occurs in “BOTH UPGAZE AND DOWNGAZE” because of restrictive ocular motility from mechanical entrapment of the inferior oblique or inferior rectus, adjacent connective tissue, or fat (L25, slide 21). The patient’s restricted elevation and worse diplopia on attempted upgaze therefore fit this mechanism. Infraorbital numbness also fits the stated “INFRAORBITAL NERVE ANAESTHESIA” when the fracture involves the infraorbital canal, while enophthalmos is listed in severe cases (L25, slide 22). Thus the combination strongly identifies an orbital-floor fracture.

B. Orbital roof is wrong because it is not the characteristic wall implicated by this blunt-trauma pattern; the course instead teaches the floor injury and its associated restrictive diplopia, infraorbital nerve anaesthesia, and enophthalmos. The lecture does not provide separate clinical features of orbital-roof fractures (not taken from the course material).

C. Medial orbital wall is wrong because, although another wall may accompany a floor fracture, the CT teaching point is “Fracture of the orbital floor ± other orbital wall,” and the vignette’s taught signs identify the floor as the principal involved wall (L25, slide 23). The lecture does not separately describe medial-wall fractures (not taken from the course material).

D. Lateral orbital wall is wrong because the described blow-out syndrome is taught as an orbital-floor fracture, not as a lateral-wall injury (L25, slide 19–22). The lecture does not separately describe the clinical presentation of lateral-wall fractures (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognize that blunt orbital trauma with restrictive vertical diplopia, infraorbital numbness, and enophthalmos indicates an orbital-floor blow-out fracture.
